title: Architecture and Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Elena Martinez
content:
Overview

This page consolidates Redwood's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure (IaC and cloud), model-serving, observability, and performance. It also defines the Decision Record (ADR) process and where ADRs are stored. The goal is to provide clear, actionable guidance for engineers and reviewers so new services and changes meet reliability, security, and cost objectives.

Scope and Goals
- Scope: All new and existing services owned by engineering teams, platform tooling, Dedicated/Private deployment packaging, and model-serving stacks.
- Goals:
  - Ensure consistent developer ergonomics and predictable runtime behavior.
  - Maintain measurable SLOs and clear ownership.
  - Reduce operational overhead with standard patterns for deployment, monitoring, and rollouts.

Principles
1. API-first: public surfaces (REST/HTTP or gRPC) should be designed as first-class products with versioning, docs, and client examples.
2. Small, well-defined contracts: keep request and response shapes explicit and schema-backed (JSON Schema / OpenAPI).
3. Observability by default: metrics, traces, structured logs, and dashboards shipped with every service.
4. Secure-in-design: least privilege, KMS for secrets, and RBAC for admin operations.
5. Performance-conscious: defaults should favor low-latency for user-facing paths and predictable unit costs for inference.

API Standards
- Surface and format:
  - Use OpenAPI v3 for HTTP JSON endpoints and protobuf + gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs.
  - All endpoints must include stable path names (no POST for idempotent fetch), use proper verbs, and semantic status codes.
- Versioning:
  - Path versioning (/v1/) for externally consumed APIs; header-based versioning allowed for internal experimental contracts.
  - Deprecation: announce 30 days in advance for internal APIs; 90 days for public hosted APIs.
- Authentication and authorization:
  - Use bearer tokens (short-lived JWTs) or mTLS for service-to-service calls. Integrate with Redwood's IAM for role checks.
- Error handling:
  - Follow the standardized error envelope: { code: string, message: string, details?: object }. Map HTTP 4xx/5xx consistently.
- Rate limiting and quotas:
  - Implement per-API and per-customer limits using shared rate-limiter library. Default soft-limit: 100 requests/sec per customer for new endpoints; tune with product.
- Schema & contract testing:
  - Publish OpenAPI and add contract tests in CI that validate request/response shapes and example fixtures.
- Example (curl + JSON schema snippet):
  - curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"Hello"}'
  - Request schema example (OpenAPI fragment):
    {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "prompt": { "type": "string" },
        "max_tokens": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 1 }
      },
      "required": ["prompt"]
    }

Coding Standards
- Languages & frameworks:
  - Primary languages: Go (services), Python (model tooling/evals), TypeScript (console/frontend). Use language-specific style guides.
- Linting & formatting:
  - Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff/mypy for Python, and prettier/eslint for TypeScript. CI must fail on formatting/lint regressions.
- Testing:
  - Unit tests required with >=80% coverage for critical path modules. Integration tests for service contracts and end-to-end model-serving flows.
- Type safety and contracts:
  - Prefer static types where available (Go, TypeScript). Python services must adopt typed signatures in public APIs.
- Dependency management:
  - Use go modules, pip-compile/poetry for Python, and npm/yarn workspaces for JS. Vendor durable dependencies for infra-critical components.
- PR checklist (must be included in PR description):
  1. Design doc / ADR linked if applicable.
  2. Unit/integration tests added.
  3. Lint/format checks passing.
  4. Load/perf impact assessed (if relevant).
  5. Observability hooks added (metrics/tracing/logging).

Infrastructure Standards
- IaC and accounts:
  - All infra must be declared in Terraform modules using the company module registry. Environments: dev, staging, prod. Cloud accounts separated per environment and team.
- Networking and VPCs:
  - Use shared VPC patterns; private subnets for workloads with egress through approved NAT gateways. No public RDP/SSH.
- Secrets and keys:
  - Use KMS-backed secret store (AWS Secrets Manager / SSM with encryption). Access via short-lived roles.
- CI/CD:
  - Every service must have an automated pipeline with: build, unit tests, integration tests, canary rollout, and automated rollback on SLO regressions.
- Tagging and cost allocation:
  - All resources must include tags: owner_team, service, env, cost_center. Cost alerts for monthly spend anomalies.

Model-serving Standards
- Model packaging & provenance:
  - Store model artifacts in the model registry with metadata: model_id, variant (quantized/float), training_commit, dataset_hash, eval_metrics, and signed checksum.
- Versioning & compatibility:
  - Semantic model versions (major.minor.patch). Minor/patch should be safe to hot-swap if backward compatible. Major requires ADR and coordinated rollout.
- Quantization and latency profiles:
  - Quantization profiles must be published in quantization-profiles directory and include accuracy delta, latency, and memory. Default rollout: test against canned evals before production.
- Serving configuration:
  - Standard serving config keys: max_seq_len, batch_size, kv_cache_enabled, max_concurrency, preferred_kernel. Provide YAML example in repo templates.
- Autoscaling and batching:
  - Autoscale by CPU/GPU utilization and request queue length. Batching strategy must preserve latency SLOs; default continuous batching enabled for throughput-oriented routes.
- Data privacy and telemetry:
  - Customer payloads must not be logged in plaintext. PII must be masked before logs or metrics emission. Ensure configs for privacy in Private deployments.
- Rollout policy:
  - Canary: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automated quality checks (latency, error rate, eval regressions). Provide automatic rollback if thresholds breached.

Observability Standards
- Metrics:
  - Export using OpenMetrics. Standard metric prefixes and labels: redwood_request_latency_seconds (le, p50,p95,p99), redwood_errors_total{code,route}, redwood_model_inference_tokens.
- Tracing:
  - Use distributed tracing with consistent trace IDs across service boundaries. Instrument critical code paths and model inference spans.
- Logs:
  - Structured JSON logs, include request_id, user_id (hashed), service, level, and canonical error codes. No plaintext PII.
- Dashboards and alerts:
  - Dashboards shipped at service and route level. Alerts:
    - SEV-1: availability below 99.9% for 5 minutes.
    - Latency: p95 > 2x baseline for 10 minutes -> Pager escalation.
    - Error budget burn: 50% of monthly budget burned in 24 hours -> Ops review.
- Retention and sampling:
  - Traces retained 30 days, logs 90 days by default; adjust for compliance workloads. Use adaptive sampling for high-volume endpoints.

Performance Standards and Benchmarking
- SLOs (default service SLOs):
  - Request latency (user-facing endpoints): p95 < 200 ms, p99 < 600 ms.
  - Model inference (text generation): p50 < 50 ms / token, p95 < 200 ms / token for low-latency models.
  - Availability: 99.95% monthly for Hosted control-plane services.
- Benchmarking process:
  - Maintain a perf-suite in eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Benchmarks include representative prompt mixes, concurrency sweeps, and warm/cold cache scenarios.
- Load testing and capacity planning:
  - Run load tests against staging with production-like request distribution. Capacity planners must submit quarterly forecasts to eng-sre.
- Profiling & kernel selection:
  - Use the profiling-playbook for identifying bottlenecks. Kernel and CUDA selection must be validated through microbenchmarks before fleet-wide changes.

ADR (Architectural Decision Record) Process
- When to write an ADR:
  - Any long-lived architectural change (new infra pattern, major model-serving change, public API versioning, or data residency decisions).
- ADR template (stored under confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-templates):
  1. Title
  2. Status (proposed | accepted | deprecated)
  3. Context (what are we solving)
  4. Options considered
  5. Decision and rationale
  6. Consequences and rollout plan
  7. Owners and reviewers
  8. Date
- Storage and discoverability:
  - ADRs must be checked into the architecture ADR registry and linked from service READMEs. Major ADRs require review by Architecture Council.

Governance and Ownership
- Owners:
  - Each service must specify an on-call owner, a code owner team, and a product owner in its README.
- Review cadence:
  - Architecture Council reviews major ADRs monthly. Standards pages (this document and sub-pages) reviewed quarterly.

Operational runbook pointers
- For incidents related to API performance or model regressions, follow the runbooks in oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks and eng-serving-runtime/runbooks. Include test prompts and canary rollback steps.

References and templates
- Templates and example configs: confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-templates, confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite, confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles.

Appendix: Quick checklists
- New service launch checklist (short):
  1. OpenAPI published and contract tests in CI.
  2. Terraform modules created and reviewed.
  3. Observability: metrics/traces/logs and dashboards.
  4. SLOs defined and alert rules in place.
  5. ADR(s) linked for major decisions.

Contacts
- Architecture Council: arch-council@redwood.ai
- Eng SRE: eng-sre@redwood.ai
- Model-serving owners: model-serving-team@redwood.ai

For any clarifications, open an RFC in the Architecture Council board and link it here.
